subject: implementer
reason: The root cause (a new request id on every post) is fixed by posting the form's stable RequestId, with a client-side submit-once guard and a server-side catch of the unique-key race. Both reuse Ordering's existing idempotency path and the WebApp's existing script pattern without crossing service or layer boundaries.

items.reason: The idempotency RequestId now comes from the browser form. Ordering's ClientRequest ids are global and not scoped to the buyer, so a crafted id that collides with an existing one is treated as a duplicate (silently 'succeeds' without an order). Any caller of Ordering.API could already set x-requestid directly.
items.fix: Optional follow-up: scope the stored request id to the buyer (or have the WebApp derive or sign it) so a client-chosen id cannot collide with another user's.

items.reason: The form is released only on Blazor's 'enhancedload'. If the enhanced post fails in a way that never fires that event, Place order stays disabled until the page is reloaded.
items.fix: Also release the form after a timeout, or on a failed fetch or error-page render.

items.title: Double-clicking Place order creates exactly one order with the bag's total
covers: Expected: a double-click places exactly one order with the bag's total
items.reason: This is the reported bug: two submits of the checkout form created two identical orders and charged the shopper twice. Only a real browser double-click exercises the submit-once script and the shared `x-requestid` together, so the case runs e2e on the test stack exactly as the ticket's reproduction steps.

items.title: After a double-click on Place order the shopping bag is empty
covers: Expected: the shopping bag is emptied after the order, as today (double-click)
items.reason: The Expected section keeps "bag emptied after the order" for the double-click flow; blocking or deduplicating the second submit must not leave the basket untouched or the checkout half-done. It is a separate observable from the order count in TC-BUG-41-01, so it gets its own case; the double-click only exists in the browser, hence e2e.

items.title: A single click on Place order creates one order and lands on My orders
covers: Expected: a single click places one order, exactly as today
Expected: the shopper lands on My orders, as today
items.reason: The fix adds a submit-once script and posts the form's `RequestId`; either could break the normal flow (form never submits, or redirect lost). The story requires the single-click flow to stay as today, and only the rendered WebApp shows the redirect, so it is e2e.

items.title: After a single click on Place order the shopping bag is empty
covers: Expected: the shopping bag is emptied after the order, as today (single click)
items.reason: The story keeps "bag emptied after the order" for the normal flow; a change to the checkout form must not stop `BasketState.CheckoutAsync` from clearing the basket. Separate from TC-BUG-41-03 because it is a different observable (basket vs. orders); e2e because the flow starts in the WebApp.

items.title: Two separate checkouts, one click each, create two orders
covers: Expected: a single click places one order, exactly as today (each new checkout gets its own order)
items.reason: The fix makes every post of one rendered checkout form share one request id, and Ordering now treats a repeated id as a duplicate. If the id were reused across separate visits to the checkout page, a shopper's second, legitimate order would silently be dropped. Today two checkouts create two orders, and the story requires single clicks to behave as today; only the WebApp renders new forms, so it is e2e.

items.title: Place order still works after the form was rejected by a validation error
covers: Expected: a single click places one order, exactly as today (form can be submitted again after a validation error)
items.reason: Today a shopper who leaves a required address field empty sees a validation message, fixes it and places the order. A submit-once guard that is not released after the server re-renders the form would leave Place order dead, a regression of the "as today" single-click flow. Only the browser runs the guard, so it is e2e.

items.title: Two concurrent order requests with the same request id create one order
covers: Expected: a double-click (a second click before the page moves on) places exactly one order — server side
items.reason: The ticket's "second click before the page moves on" can reach the server when the browser guard does not run (script not yet loaded, enhanced navigation bypassed). Both posts then carry the same `x-requestid`; if Ordering lets both inserts race, the shopper is charged twice. An accepted order cannot be saved in the Ordering functional host, so this API-level case runs on the test stack (e2e layer, API calls as `alice`).
